findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Capital Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix B
findings.headline: The £29.205m capital programme is forecast to underspend by £773k (2.6%), with variances driven by lower demand rather than delivery failures.
findings.detail: Q1 actual spending of £3.215m represents 11% of the revised full-year budget. Forecast outturn is £28.432m. Multiple schemes show underspends due to lower demand: Disabled Facilities Grants £143k under (grant exceeds demand), Neighbourhoods £364k under (reduced vehicle replacement need with cost savings found), and Health & Wellbeing Hub £232k under. These are demand-driven variations, not delivery constraints.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether capital spending variations reflect delivery delays or demand fluctuations. Underspends driven by lower demand indicate the council is responsive to actual service needs and managing finances effectively.
findings.figures: £29.205m budget, £28.432m forecast, £773k underspend (2.6%), £3.215m Q1 actual
findings.quote: SHDC have historically underspent DFGs as grant received outstrips demand.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Capital Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix B
findings.headline: Capital Enhancements schemes are largely on hold, with only the Spalding Cemetery Expansion proceeding in the current financial year.
findings.detail: The £184k Capital Enhancements budget is forecast to spend only £150k, indicating that schemes other than the cemetery expansion have been deferred. The document does not explain the reasons for deferral or planned timings for the deferred schemes.
findings.matters: Although the Capital Enhancements budget is small relative to the total programme (£184k of £29.2m), the deferral of multiple schemes may indicate resource constraints or other factors a lender would want to understand.
findings.figures: £184k budget, £150k forecast, £34k underspend
findings.quote: Capital Enhancements – Spalding Cemetery Expansion only scheme currently forecast to be moving forward within current financial year with other schemes on hold.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Capital Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix B
findings.headline: The £16.708m Health & Wellbeing Hub, representing 57% of the capital programme, is progressing on track for early 2027 completion and opening.
findings.detail: By end Q1, the project had spent £2.747m of a forecast total of £16.476m. The document reports positive physical progress including pool tank formation and testing, internal configuration progressing, and contractor appointment imminent for the 3G pitch. The project is forecast to complete with a minor £232k underspend.
findings.matters: The Health & Wellbeing Hub is by far the largest capital investment in the council's programme. A lender would monitor the council's ability to deliver major projects on schedule, and positive progress confirms adequate project governance and delivery capability.
findings.figures: £16.708m budget, £2.747m Q1 spend, £16.476m forecast
findings.quote: Positive progress continues. New pool tanks are formed and being tested for water tightness. New internal configuration taking shape. Tenders for 3G pitch construction completed to enable contractor appointment. Scheme progress is on track for early 2027 completion and opening.

findings.matters: Strong collection ahead of profile indicates healthy cash flow and residents' ability to pay. Early outperformance provides financial flexibility and reduces revenue shortfall risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Sports Centre closed September 2025; council now operates from temporary facility with reduced capacity.
findings.detail: The Sports Centre closed in September 2025 and the council is currently delivering leisure services from a temporary facility with reduced capacity, limited equipment, and restricted activity program. Several dryside activities and bowls are unavailable. Despite constraints, participation has been maintained relatively well.
findings.matters: Closure of a major asset indicates capital pressures or planned works. Ongoing operation from temporary facilities carries higher interim costs and risks extended service disruption, affecting debt repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Visitor numbers Q1: 27,547 (vs 84,226 in Q1 prior year); gym members: 845; swimming lesson participation: 19,433
findings.quote: Since the Sports Centre closed in September 2025, performance has remained strong despite operating from a temporary facility with reduced capacity, limited equipment, and a restricted activity programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Household waste recycling at 35%, 10 points below target, with new collection model planned.
findings.detail: Recycling and composting collection achieved 35.19% in 2025/26 against a 45% target (marked L for below target). The council is progressing a revised waste collection model including transition from sack collections to wheeled bins and enhanced recycling provision, expected to improve future performance. This will require capital investment.
findings.matters: Environmental compliance shortfall could lead to regulatory pressure. The planned remediation requires capital investment in collection vehicles and infrastructure, creating a capital claim on council resources.
findings.figures: 35.19% achieved against 45% target (marked L)
findings.quote: Recycling and composting performance was 35% for the 25/26 year, below the target of 45%. To address this, the Council is progressing plans for a revised waste collection model, including the move from sack collections to wheeled bins and enhanced recycling provision.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Voluntary staff turnover more than doubled from 2.25% in Q4 to 4.79% in Q1.
findings.detail: Voluntary staff turnover jumped from 2.25% in Q4 to 4.79% in Q1, a 113% quarter-on-quarter increase. Total cumulative turnover rose by 3.49% in Q1 alone. Of leavers, 83% were classified as voluntary (including 3 retirements). The council experienced a high volume of departures.
findings.matters: Rapid staff departure disrupts institutional knowledge and service continuity. High turnover during a period of governance stress (complaints failures) suggests workplace or management problems affecting staff morale.
findings.figures: 4.79% voluntary turnover (Q1) vs 2.25% (Q4); 3.49 percentage point increase in cumulative turnover
findings.quote: Total turnover has increased by 3.49% and the voluntary turnover has increased by 2.54% up to 4.79% compared to the previous quarter.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Health and Safety compliance actions only 76% complete, missing 100% target.
findings.detail: Percentage of Health and Safety audit and inspection actions completed partnership-wide within timescale was 76% against a 100% target (marked L for below target). At SHDC one action remained overdue: 'H&S monitoring and supervision of facilities staff team' had no evidence of records monitoring compliance with Risk Assessment and Safe Systems of work, though this was later closed 23 July 2026.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with Health and Safety obligations creates regulatory risk and potential liability. Failure to close out compliance actions on time indicates management weakness.
findings.figures: 76.00% completed (target 100%, marked L)
findings.quote: H&S monitoring and supervision of facilities staff team. No evidence of records monitoring compliance with Risk Assessment and Safe Systems of work. Closed as of 23/07/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Waste collection first-time success fell to 94.99%, triggering significant missed pickups in Q1.
findings.detail: First-time collection success rate dropped from 99.86% in Q4 to 94.99%, missing the 99.80% target. Disruption followed bank holidays in April and May (specifically 4 May and 24 May) when collections reverted to Saturday. An extended road closure on Surfleet Road in Pinchbeck generated 268 missed collection reports with spillover into Gosberton (140 reports). Collections recovered in June, falling 42% compared with April.
findings.matters: Service delivery failures increase complaints, reputational damage, and potential liabilities. Poor contingency planning for foreseeable disruptions like bank holidays indicates operational fragility.
findings.figures: 94.99% vs 99.80% target; 268 missed reports (Pinchbeck/West Pinchbeck); 140 missed reports (Gosberton); 42% reduction in June vs April
findings.quote: Higher volumes of missed collections were reported following the bank holiday periods in April and May, specifically after Monday 4th May and Monday 24th May, as collections reverted to Saturday rather than moving forward by one day.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Verified rough sleepers jumped from 8 to 25, a 212% surge in one quarter.
findings.detail: The count of verified rough sleepers increased sharply from 8 in Q4 to 25 in Q1, indicating a dramatic deterioration in homelessness. This suggests financial distress among vulnerable residents and signals potential budget pressures if homelessness support services must expand.
findings.matters: A rapid surge in rough sleepers indicates worsening economic conditions and reduced ability of residents to afford housing. This creates demand pressure on council services and may affect collection rates and resident financial resilience more broadly.
findings.figures: 25 in Q1 vs 8 in Q4 (previous year)
findings.quote: Number of verified rough sleepers 11 19 14 8 25

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Q1 SHDC Performance Report
findings.headline: Corporate complaints handling collapsed to 40%, down from 95% target.
findings.detail: The percentage of corporate complaints responded to within timescale fell from 76.92% in Q4 to 40% in Q1. The council attributes this to 'operational delays and availability of officers to respond', indicating a significant internal capacity or management problem. This represents a governance failure.
findings.matters: Failure to respond to complaints is a red flag for management dysfunction. It signals loss of control over basic operations and suggests wider organisational stress that could affect service delivery and financial management.
findings.figures: 40.00% achieved (Q1) against 95% target; marked L (below target)
findings.quote: Service area responses due to operational delays and availability of officers to respond as key performance impact.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Covering Report SHDC
findings.headline: Investment position declining with cash and equivalents down £2.956m in first quarter
findings.detail: The council's cash and investments declined from £29.031m on 31 March 2026 to £26.075m on 30 June 2026, a material reduction in the first quarter. The council is also drawing planned reserves from Waste Transformation, Investment and Growth, and Planning reserves.
findings.matters: Declining reserves indicate the council is using liquid funds to manage its finances; if the trend continues, the council's financial flexibility for future borrowing or unexpected costs will be constrained.
findings.figures: £29.031m (31 March 2026); £26.075m (30 June 2026); decline of approximately £2.956m
findings.quote: Investments including cash and cash equivalents held by the Council on 30 June 2026 (excluding accrued interest) totalled £ 26.075m compared with £2 9.031m on 31 March 2026.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Covering Report SHDC
findings.headline: HRA premature debt repayment in March 2026 driving material one-off accounting benefit
findings.detail: The council completed premature repayment of Housing Revenue Account debt in March 2026, creating a £1.588m favorable variance. The primary driver is the accounting treatment of the early redemption, allocating the discount to revenue over 10 years, resulting in an annual accounting credit of £1.837m.
findings.matters: A lender cares about debt management decisions; early repayment demonstrates market access and deliberate financial management, but the favorable variance is a one-off accounting treatment not indicative of ongoing operational performance.
findings.figures: £1.588m favorable variance; £1.837m annual credit
findings.quote: The primary driver of this favourable position is the premature repayment of debt completed in March 2026 and the discount allocated to revenue over 10 years resulting in an annual credit of £1.837m.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Covering Report SHDC
findings.headline: Service cost pressures of £682,000 offset by investment income gains that are likely temporary
findings.detail: The council reports a £17,000 General Fund surplus, but underlying service costs are £682,000 over budget, offset by investment income beating budget by £432,000 and minimum revenue provision savings of £267,000. The investment income outperformance is driven by interest rates remaining higher than budgeted and will normalize as rates fall.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council has structural cost issues masked by temporary investment gains; as interest rates fall, the council will face deficit without cost reductions or revenue growth.
findings.figures: service pressures £682,000; investment income outperformance £432,000; MRP saving £267,000; net position £17,000 surplus
findings.quote: there are service pressures of £ 682,000 across cost of services which are offset by forecast overachievement of investment income of £432,000 and minimum revenue provision saving of £267,000.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Debt collection remains challenging due to cost of living crisis, with £257k in sundry debts outstanding for over 365 days.
findings.detail: The council reports that collection and recovery remain challenging in 2026/27 due to ongoing cost of living pressures and continues to maintain prudent bad debt provisions. Of £839,795 in total sundry debt, £257,208 (31%) is outstanding for over 365 days, representing aged and potentially unrecoverable debt.
findings.matters: Deteriorating debt collection directly reduces cash inflow and income; councils facing cost of living pressure typically see lower recovery rates and higher bad debt provisioning requirements.
findings.figures: Debts over 365 days: £257,208; total sundry debt £839,795; additional uninvoiced items £109,114
findings.quote: Collection and recovery remain challenging in 2026/27 due to the ongoing cost of living crisis.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Council has budgeted to borrow £1m on 1 October 2026 at 3.50% if surplus cash is not available.
findings.detail: The council notes it will borrow £1m at fixed 3.50% on 1 October 2026 conditional on not having surplus cash at that date. The conditional framing suggests uncertainty about cash position and liquidity headroom without external funding.
findings.matters: Conditional borrowing indicates potential liquidity pressures despite the reported surplus position, raising questions about underlying cash generation.
findings.figures: £1.000m borrowing planned; rate 3.50%
findings.quote: The Council has budgeted to borrow £1.000m on 1 October 2026 at a rate of 3.50%. If the Council has surplus cash on 1 October 2026 this borrowing will not be taken until required.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: General Fund reserves are being drawn down to fund revenue and capital expenditure, with significant use of earmarked reserves.
findings.detail: General Fund reserves are forecast at £11.275m as at 31 March 2027. Specific reserves show material drawdowns: Investment and Growth reserve down £806k, Planning reserve down £250k, Waste Transformation reserve down £1.280m. A net use of reserves of £324k is made in Q1 alone to cover revenue and capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Use of earmarked reserves to fund recurrent expenditure is not sustainable; if structural pressures persist, reserves will deplete quickly.
findings.figures: Total reserves £11.275m forecast; Q1 net use £324k; specific reserves: Investment and Growth (down £806k), Planning (down £250k), Waste Transformation (down £1.280m)
findings.quote: As of 30 June 2026, the forecast General Fund reserve balance is £11.275m, after a net use of reserves of £0.324m to cover revenue and capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: The forecast £17k surplus depends entirely on capital programme slippage, with uninvested cash creating investment income and reducing MRP provisions.
findings.detail: The council's reported year-end surplus of £17k is achieved only because capital spending is not happening as planned. Capital slippage generates £432k in additional investment income and £267k in MRP reduction, totalling £699k in positive variances. Without these slippage benefits, the £682k in service cost pressures would result in a substantial deficit. This means the underlying operational position masks structural cost overruns.
findings.matters: The balanced forecast is not sustainable; it depends on projects not being delivered and cash not being spent rather than operational control.
findings.figures: Service pressures £682k; capital slippage creating £432k additional investment income and £267k MRP reduction; net forecast surplus £17k
findings.quote: Additional investment income is anticipated due to slippage in the delivery of the capital programme. Favourable variance due to the slippage in the previous year's delivery of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 GF Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix A
findings.headline: Service budgets assume salary efficiency savings that are not being achieved across multiple services, requiring expensive agency staffing instead.
findings.detail: Forecast service cost pressures of £682k are primarily driven by staffing costs. Unmet salary efficiency targets are reported across six services: Neighbourhoods (£103k), Planning & Strategic Infrastructure (£62k), Regulatory (£52k), Communities and Housing Services (£78k), Finance (£39k), and Strategic Growth & Development (£10k). Neighbourhoods additionally reports £174k of agency costs to fill staffing gaps.
findings.matters: Budget planning assumptions about salary reductions are not materialising; if not achieved, these pressures will persist through the year.
findings.figures: £682k total service pressures; unmet targets £39k, £103k, £62k, £52k, £78k, £10k across services; £174k agency costs in Neighbourhoods
findings.quote: Table 1 shows forecast service pressures of £682k across Cost of Services, primarily arising from staffing costs, including agency expenditure and the unmet salary efficiency target.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 HRA Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix C
findings.headline: HRA General Reserve declines 45% from £12.069m to £6.668m as capital programme funding is drawn from accumulated reserves
findings.detail: Net reserve use is £5.482m to fund £27.517m capital spend, primarily £13.694m renewable energy programme. Reserve decline is strategic and temporary (future capital programmes £11–15m annually versus this year's peak £27.517m), reflecting concentrated investment funded from accumulated balances and grants.
findings.matters: A 45% single-year reserve decline is material and constrains financial buffer. While the draw reflects planned capital investment rather than deficit funding, sustained draws at this rate would deplete the closing £6.668m balance within one to two years.
findings.figures: Opening reserve £12.069m, closing £6.668m, net use £5.482m, capital spend £27.517m
findings.quote: As of 30 June 2026, the forecast HRA reserve balance is £7.248m, after a net use of reserves of £5.482m to cover revenue and capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Q1 HRA Finance Report 2026-27 Appendix C
findings.headline: HRA debt repaid early in March 2026: £67.456m redeemed at discount and £50m new PWLB borrowing agreed, reducing net debt by £17.456m
findings.detail: The early repayment generated £1.837m discount allocated to revenue. Budget had assumed £67.456m external borrowing; this was replaced with £50m PWLB borrowing, with a further £7m budgeted at 3.50% from 1 October 2026 if needed. The transaction reduced overall HRA borrowing while securing lower-cost replacement funding.
findings.matters: A £17.456m net debt reduction indicates the council had liquidity to refinance at improved rates. The redemption discount shows favourable early repayment terms were secured, lowering the long-term cost of HRA funding.
findings.figures: £67.456m repaid, £1.837m redemption discount to revenue, £50m replacement borrowing, £7m additional at 3.50%, net debt reduction £17.456m
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget assumed HRA external borrowing of £67.456m. In March 2026 this was prematurely repaid at a discount, and £50m of new borrowing was agreed with the Public Works Loan Board.

findings.detail: Government awarded further £1 million in June 2026 to support Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards (MEES) programme. Business plan models delivery of EPC C rating by 2030 for approximately 1000 properties through contracts awarded for works until 2028. Risk score improved from Medium (9) to Low (4).

findings.headline: Emergency repairs staffing crisis resolved through statutory terms change, risk downgraded from High to Low
findings.detail: Council adopted proposals in February 2026 to change emergency repair operatives' terms and conditions to enable mandatory on-call availability. New rota commenced September 2026. Previous risk was high due to insufficient 24/7 staffing for emergency repairs, creating Awaab's law breach risk. Risk score improved from High (12) to Low (1).
findings.matters: Emergency repairs directly impact tenant safety and regulatory compliance; inability to respond within call-out window creates statutory breach risk, potential litigation, and reputational damage.

findings.quote: Council adopted proposals in Feb 26 to change terms and conditions for staff. Necessary paperwork issued to staff, new rota commences September 2026

findings.headline: Regulatory grading at C2, improvement trajectory announced but summer 2026 target status unclear
findings.detail: Housing Regulator (RSH) issued C2 grading on 25 July, with monthly meetings held since to track improvement. Council states working towards C1 with anticipated summer 2026 achievement. Document dated September 2026 does not confirm whether C1 was reached, leaving regulatory standing ambiguous.
findings.matters: Regulatory grading signals control environment strength to lenders; C2 indicates areas requiring improvement, while C1 is standard oversight level.
findings.figures: C2 grading issued 25 July; target for C1 improvement stated as summer 2026

findings.paper_title: SHDC Appendix B Q1 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Recent internal audits confirm adequate governance and control assurance
findings.detail: Internal audits on health and safety compliance and on workforce capacity and change readiness have both provided 'Adequate Assurance' ratings. The council has completed all audit recommendations on schedule. This provides confirmation that key governance and control frameworks are functioning appropriately despite the council's significant operational workload and change agenda.
findings.matters: Adequate audit assurance directly indicates whether the council's financial and operational controls are effective and being actively managed. This supports confidence in the council's governance capability to manage budget and service delivery risks.
findings.figures: Health and Safety audit: Adequate Assurance; Capacity audit: Adequate Assurance

findings.paper_title: SHDC Appendix B Q1 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Environment Act 2021 compliance has unresolved ongoing funding gap
findings.detail: South Holland must comply with Environment Act 2021 requirements affecting waste service delivery, assessed as High (16) current risk. The council has received some New Burdens funding but explicitly states that ongoing funding is uncertain. The target is to reduce this to Medium (9) by 30 September 2026. Governance is in place via a Waste Improvement Programme Board and Steering Group chaired by the Portfolio Holder.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can fund statutory compliance. The ongoing funding gap for Environment Act compliance remains unresolved and represents a potential unfunded service cost, even as the council actively manages the implementation.
findings.figures: Current risk High (16), target Medium (9), deadline 30/09/2026
findings.quote: although some New Burdens has been made available information is not provided on the ongoing New Burdens revenue funding to meet the additional cost of service delivery

findings.paper_title: SHDC Appendix B Q1 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: EPR waste scheme funding now confirmed, removing budget pressure
findings.detail: The Extended Producer Responsibility scheme was previously a source of budget uncertainty for waste collection funding. The government has now guaranteed £1.1 billion across all local authorities to fund packaging waste collection. South Holland has received formal notification of its confirmed funding allocation. The council's risk score for this item has been reduced in Q2.
findings.matters: Removes a previously unresolved budget pressure and confirms revenue for a core service. The government guarantee provides funding certainty that allows the council to plan effectively rather than bracing for service cost cuts.

This assurance helps local councils plan their budgets effectively. SHDC has received notification of payment for 2025/26 - £1,231,000

findings.paper_title: SHDC Appendix B Q1 Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Budget balancing risk remains persistently high with no planned improvement
findings.detail: South Holland identifies budget risk as High (16) with a target remaining at High (16), indicating no planned risk reduction. The council lists multiple pressures: government funding reduction, income reduction, capital expenditure, Internal Drainage Board levy pressures (the subject of active lobbying), inflation, fuel costs, and residual impacts from the Ukraine conflict. Mitigation relies on a Medium Term Financial Strategy, budgetary process discipline, a 'sound level of reserves', and continued monitoring.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's creditworthiness needs to understand budget sustainability. A persistent High risk with static outlook suggests ongoing structural pressures despite existing mitigations, particularly the external IDB levy pressure which the council cannot directly control.
findings.figures: Budget risk score High (16), unchanged from current to target
findings.quote: Reduction of government funding; Reduction in income; Capital expenditure; Impact of Internal Drainage Board (IDB) levy; Inflation; Fuel shortages; Ukraine conflict

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Q1 Partnership Risk Registers
findings.headline: Staffing resilience risk is improving as the partnership implements workforce development and capacity management initiatives, with risk reduction targeted for end-Q2 2026.
findings.detail: The partnership identifies staff retention and resilience as a current High risk (12) but targets Medium (9) by 30/09/2026. Mitigations include a new managers development programme, recruitment academy, Future Leaders' Programme, and offer to allow services to bid into the transformation/capacity reserve for short-term support. The register notes that 'email appears to be the biggest pressure' on staff and plans a 'refresh of the Workforce Development Strategy action plan this year, in light of LGR, to help ensure colleagues have the skills and confidence required to continue to want to work in Local Government post re-organisation.'
findings.matters: Staffing stability supports the councils' financial management capacity and ability to execute the savings plan identified in the funding risk; turnover and recruitment costs affect the cost base.
findings.figures: Risk score High (12) reducing to Medium (9) by 30/09/2026
findings.quote: A refresh of the Workforce Development Strategy action plan will take place this year, in light of LGR, to help ensure colleagues have the skills and confidence required to continue to want to work in Local Government post re-organisation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Q1 Partnership Risk Registers
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty remains a high unmitigated risk affecting leadership capacity and service delivery, with no planned risk reduction.
findings.detail: The register identifies that LGR 'will create a prolonged period of uncertainty impacting organisational culture, workforce stability, leadership capacity and change readiness, as well as service delivery and community confidence.' The councils submitted an LGR proposal and are 'awaiting the outcome.' The risk score remains High (12) with no improvement to the target; the planned action is to 'continue to work with other Councils to ensure our Councils and Greater Lincolnshire are well positioned for LGR, regardless of proposal to be implemented.'
findings.matters: LGR creates structural uncertainty that could impair the councils' capacity to manage finances, retain leadership, and deliver services—material to any lender's assessment of council stability and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Risk score High (12), unchanged from current to target
findings.quote: Local Government Reorganisation will create a prolonged period of uncertainty impacting organisational culture, workforce stability, leadership capacity and change readiness, as well as service delivery and community confidence.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C Q1 Partnership Risk Registers
findings.headline: South Holland's partnership councils have identified funding gaps and are pursuing efficiency savings through the partnership business case, with risk reduction targeted for end-Q2 2026.
findings.detail: The risk register explicitly identifies 'Local Government funding challenges are inevitable and evidenced by each partner's funding gaps.' The partnership business case is designed to deliver 'a significant opportunity to respond to this on-going challenge' through shared services and commercial opportunities. The treatment plan is to realise 'the planned savings' through a savings tracker monitored by the Transformation Board, reviewed quarterly. The funding risk is targeted to reduce from High (16) to Medium (9) by 30/09/2026.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether councils can sustain operations and service debt obligations given identified funding pressures; this paper shows explicit recognition of gaps and an active mitigation plan with a near-term target date.
findings.figures: Risk score High (16) reducing to Medium (9) by 30/09/2026

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: MRP policy defers charges on Welland Homes equity using annuity method over 50 years, concentrating cost to later years
findings.detail: The council is charging MRP on its £3.705m Welland Homes share capital using an annuity method (deferred charges) over 50 years at the PWLB annuity rate, not a straight-line method. The guidance notes this method is used 'where the flow of benefits from an asset are expected to increase in later years,' but a housing stock typically has stable benefits, not increasing ones. This defers revenue charges and increases future financial commitments.
findings.matters: Annuity MRP is less conservative and loads costs into the outer years of the forecast, when other commitments may be tighter. For a lender assessing medium-term sustainability, deferred charges mask near-term pressure and concentrate risk.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: Council has £10.25m invested in Welland Homes, a commercial property venture, outside standard treasury rules
findings.detail: The council has issued £6.546m in loans to Welland Homes and holds £3.705m in share capital (equity). These are classified as 'non-treasury investments' and sit outside normal investment limits. Welland Homes loans are being managed through MRP using projected loan repayments rather than statutory provision. The council sought 'independent professional opinion' on the useful life of the underlying housing assets.
findings.matters: A large, illiquid equity stake in a housing company introduces credit risk and liquidity risk. If Welland Homes runs into difficulty, the council has limited recourse. The special MRP treatment (deferring charges to loan repayments) also concentrates cash flow risk in future years.
findings.figures: Loans to Welland Homes: £6.546m at 31 December 2025; Share capital: £3.705m; MRP 2026/27: £14k (only 14k on 3.7m equity)
findings.quote: In addition to the above the Council has issued loans to Welland Homes totalling £6.546m at 31 December 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: Council maintains £31.9m under-borrowed position, betting on interest rates falling from current 4.81–6.01% PWLB rates
findings.detail: The council is deliberately holding reserves to defer borrowing, wagering that PWLB rates will fall. MUFG forecasts 5-year PWLB rates at 4.81% now, declining to 4.10% by end of 2027. If this forecast is wrong and rates rise instead, the council will face higher borrowing costs and may be forced to borrow at unfavourable rates to meet its capital programme.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecasting risk is material. If the council misjudges and rates rise, it incurs avoidable debt service cost increases. The under-borrowing position is not conservative; it is a directional bet on the economy.
findings.figures: Under / (over) borrowing 2026/27: £31,920k; Current PWLB 5-year certainty rate: 4.81%; Target (end Q4 2027): 4.10%
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: Capital financing need jumps 414% in a single year, driven by Large Urban Fund projects
findings.detail: Net financing need for the year is forecast to rise from £3.879m in 2025/26 to £19.952m in 2026/27 — a £16m jump in one year. This is primarily driven by Large Urban Fund (LUF) projects increasing from £10.163m to £15.511m. The Council is making a very significant capital commitment that will require substantial borrowing.
findings.matters: A sudden four-fold increase in capital financing need signals major new commitments and associated borrowing. This increases the council's debt service costs and financial risk profile materially.
findings.figures: Net financing need 2025/26: £3.879m; 2026/27: £19.952m; LUF Projects increase from £10.163m to £15.511m
findings.quote: Net financing need for the year 3,879 19,952 6,238 5,216 9,332 5,738

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4b Treasury Management Strategy Statement, MRP Policy Statement & AIS
findings.headline: HRA debt growing to unsustainable levels against revenue, climbing from 357% to 449% of revenue over five years
findings.detail: The council's Housing Revenue Account debt is forecast to grow from £67.5m to £98.5m by 2030/31, while revenues grow from £18.9m to £21.9m. The debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorates from 357% to 449%, and debt per dwelling rises from £17,668 to £26,318. This trajectory is not financially sustainable and represents an accelerating commitment.
findings.matters: For a lender, rising debt-to-revenue ratios are a primary risk indicator. A council where housing debt exceeds revenues by nearly 5x is exposed to service disruption risk and leaves no headroom for income shocks.
findings.figures: HRA debt £m: 67.456 (2025/26) to 98.456 (2030/31); ratio of debt to revenues %: 357 to 449; debt per dwelling £: 17,668 to 26,318
findings.quote: Ratio of debt to revenues % 357 380 394 410 433 449

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Treasury function is being relied upon to contribute to revenue budget relief.
findings.detail: The strategy states treasury management 'will be expected to make a positive contribution towards both revenue and capital pressures'. The council holds approximately £35m in average cash holdings and is counting on investment returns to help absorb the revenue budget gap.
findings.matters: Using treasury returns to cover structural budget deficits is unsustainable. Investment returns are volatile and cannot reliably offset growing budget pressures, signalling the council is looking to short-term measures rather than structural solutions.
findings.figures: Surplus cash averages approximately £35m
findings.quote: Treasury management will be expected to make a positive contribution towards both revenue and capital pressures.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council is planning new borrowing to fund capital investment amid growing revenue pressures.
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly states the council 'needs to consider ways of innovation that limit the amount of investment required during the timescale of this strategy in light of the significant pressures upon its resources, which will include new borrowing'. This signals intent to borrow for capital purposes.
findings.matters: New borrowing adds debt servicing costs and future Minimum Revenue Provision obligations to a budget already under growing pressure. A lender must assess whether the council can afford repayment.
findings.figures: New borrowing amount unspecified in this strategy
findings.quote: The Council also needs to consider ways of innovation that limit the amount of investment required during the timescale of this strategy in light of the significant pressures upon its resources, which will include new borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Business rate retention changes create significantly higher risk to a core income stream.
findings.detail: Changes to the localised business rate retention system are flagged as an area of focus, with the council concerned about yield changes from economic impacts and recent government policy. The document explicitly states this income stream now 'has a significantly higher level of risk'.
findings.matters: Business rates are a core council revenue source. Higher risk to this stream directly threatens revenue budget stability and the ability to service new debt.
findings.figures: Risk impact unquantified
findings.quote: so this income stream has a significantly higher level of risk. There are no signs of an upturn in Council or indeed Government finances to provide optimism.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Council holds limited general and specific reserves to weather financial shocks.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it holds 'limited levels' of both general and specific reserves, meaning minimal financial buffers to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls without borrowing.
findings.matters: Limited reserves signal weak financial resilience. A council cannot absorb service pressures or unexpected costs without emergency borrowing, increasing debt and revenue obligations.
findings.figures: Reserves described only as 'limited' (unquantified)
findings.quote: South Holland District Council holds limited levels of both general and specific reserves.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Capital Strategy
findings.headline: Revenue budget balancing is becoming harder each year through to 2030/31 with no expected improvement.
findings.detail: The council states that 'each year the ability to balance the budget is becoming more challenging' through 2030/31, driven by inflationary pressures, reduced post-COVID income, and business rate changes. The document explicitly notes 'there are no signs of an upturn in Council or indeed Government finances to provide optimism', forcing difficult choices between efficiency, income raising, and service reduction.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can sustain balanced budgets. Growing annual challenges indicate deteriorating financial resilience and increased risk of future deficits or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: Budget pressures through 2030/31
findings.quote: Each year the ability to balance the budget is becoming more challenging, with options ranging from becoming more efficient, raising additional income and/or reducing services.

findings.paper_title: DRAFT_SHDC_ISA260 14.01.2026
findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatements of £623k remain in the draft accounts
findings.detail: KPMG identified three misstatements management did not correct: £333k computer licence accrual error (£5k factual + £328k projected), £191k property understatement, and £99k car park valuation error. These would decrease the deficit by £623k if corrected. KPMG formally requests their correction per ISA 450.
findings.matters: While individually immaterial, management chose not to correct identified errors, suggesting either resource constraints or lack of rigour in closure. The pattern (accruals, valuations) indicates control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £623k total uncorrected; £333k licence; £191k PPE; £99k car park
findings.quote: In line with ISA (UK) 450 we request that you correct uncorrected misstatements. However, they will have no effect on the opinion in our auditor's report, individually or in aggregate.

findings.paper_title: DRAFT_SHDC_ISA260 14.01.2026
findings.headline: Formal record of decisions on efficiency savings does not exist, yet the Council needs to achieve £1m-£1.8m annual savings
findings.detail: Cabinet meetings held to discuss savings produced a list reviewed by Senior Leadership Team, but no minutes or action logs were kept. Business and Efficiency Savings meetings are not minuted. Internal Audit found insufficient controls in place for identification and monitoring of savings. The approved budget requires £1m savings in 2025/26, rising to £1.8m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Significant savings targets exist but governance over delivery is absent. Without formal tracking or committee oversight, the Council risks missing targets and facing budget deficits, directly affecting debt serviceability and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £1m savings required 2025/26; £1.8m required by 2028/29
findings.quote: We confirmed that a meeting was held with the Cabinet members to discuss savings before the 2024-25 budget was set. A list of potential savings was identified and discussed at this meeting, which was subject to review by the Senior Leadership Team (SLT). We requested evidence of this meeting however no minutes or actions logs have been kept by the Council.

findings.paper_title: DRAFT_SHDC_ISA260 14.01.2026
findings.headline: £1.1m of property assets cannot be accurately verified due to missing floor plan data
findings.detail: Of 40 floor areas used in property valuations, 8 (20%) did not have supporting floor plans. Of these, 2 assets totalling £1.1m could not be verified at all. Additionally, 6 other assets had correctable errors totalling £191k in understatement. This weakness was raised in the prior year and not resolved.
findings.matters: Property valuations represent the largest asset on a council balance sheet. Nearly £1.2m cannot be reliably verified, undermining calculations for reserves and debt capacity. The fact this issue persisted from prior year suggests weak management controls.
findings.figures: £1.1m unverifiable; £191k understatement; 8 out of 40 floor areas (20%) unsupported; Other Land and Buildings total £28.06m
findings.quote: We identified that there are 8 out of 40 floor areas used in the valuation that were not supported by adequate floor plans or did not exist. 2 of the 8 we could not verify which have a value of £1.1m

findings.paper_title: DRAFT_SHDC_ISA260 14.01.2026
findings.headline: The auditors are disclaiming their opinion on the financial statements due to insufficient evidence over reserves
findings.detail: KPMG cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 before the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026. They cite this as pervasive to the Council's financial position. This is a continuation of prior-year disclaimer opinions for 2023/24 and 2022/23.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditors cannot confirm the Council's financial position. For lenders, this means the true asset base, liability position, and debt serviceability cannot be independently verified. This pattern across three years suggests structural audit issues.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 12 February 2025 for 2023/24; disclaimer continuing for 2024/25 due to 27 February 2026 backstop date
findings.quote: Given our work to rebuild assurance is not fully complete and due to the statutory backstop date of 27 February 2026, we have determined that there is insufficient time to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence over the split of useable and unusable reserves as at 31 March 2025 or 31 March 2024 ahead of the backstop

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Sector-wide financial stress with £2.2bn projected black hole in councils' HRA budgets by 2028, creating macro-level risk context
findings.detail: Over 100 stock-holding councils, including South Holland, have signed the 'securing the future of social housing' campaign raising concerns about HRA financial danger, with £2.2bn projected deficit expected by 2028 nationally.
findings.matters: This shows South Holland is operating within a sector under acute financial stress; any deterioration in council finances or sector-wide factors (rents policy, voids, inflation) could impact this council's position rapidly.
findings.figures: £2.2bn black hole expected by 2028; 100+ councils signed campaign
findings.quote: In 2024, more than 100 stock holding Councils (including South Holland) signed up to the 'securing the future of social housing' campaign raising concerns about the danger of HRA finances, with a £2.2bn black hole in councils' national housing budgets expected by 2028.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: PWLB interest rates have trebled in three years, creating volatile assumptions in a 30-year plan
findings.detail: The business plan is built on current PWLB borrowing rates described as being at 'three times what they were less than 3 years ago'. The plan treats borrowing as 'financing of last resort' but this high-rate environment significantly increases the cost of the £142m new borrowing.
findings.matters: Interest rate assumptions are critical to 30-year HRA viability; rates at three-times historical levels mean further rises would materially impact affordability and headroom against the minimum 1.25 ICR threshold.
findings.figures: PWLB rates three times higher than three years ago
findings.quote: Continued high levels of interest rates available from the PWLB (at three times what they were less than 3 years ago)

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard and revised Decent Homes Standard both anticipated for 2026 implementation, driving £3.7m additional cost commitment
findings.detail: Government consultations on MEES and Decent Homes changes are expected to result in implementation during 2026. The council has already committed £3.7m in additional energy efficiency programmes to achieve EPC C rating for all stock by 2030, with these programmes commencing in 2027.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance deadlines are external cost drivers outside the council's control; the 2026 implementation date is imminent and the council's ability to deliver £3.7m of efficiency programmes while managing other pressures will test HRA headroom.
findings.figures: £3.7m additional energy efficiency programmes; EPC C target by 2030
findings.quote: Government consultations on changes to the Decent Homes Standard and the introduction of a Minimum Energy Efficiency Standard (MEES) anticipated to be implemented during 2026. Investment into energy efficiency extended to achieve EPC C for all stock by 2030. Additional programmes totalling £3.7m commencing during 2027

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Interest Cover Ratio operating at minimum regulatory threshold of 1.25, leaving tight headroom for unexpected cost increases
findings.detail: The business plan meets the 'golden rule' requirement of an Interest Cover Ratio of at least 1.25, but operates at this minimum threshold rather than with significant headroom. Any adverse movement in costs or income could breach this requirement.
findings.matters: Operating at minimum regulatory thresholds leaves little buffer for external shocks (interest rate rises, inflation, void rates); lenders typically want to see headroom above minimum requirements.
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio of at least 1.25
findings.quote: The Plan is fully financed across the 30 years, remaining within the 'golden rule' of an Interest Cover Ratio of at least 1.25%, so that there is a cushion to ensure interest can be paid in the event of unexpected cost increases.

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: Management and repair costs at 63p per £1 of rent collected — explicitly above benchmarks for similar councils
findings.detail: The paper identifies that within 2026/27, net costs of management and repairs consume 63p of every £1 of rent income after service charges and non-rent income. The council explicitly states this is 'relatively high compared to benchmarks' and flags it needs efficiency improvements.
findings.matters: Above-benchmark operating costs are a warning sign; the council has acknowledged it and says it will 'keep opportunities to seek greater efficiencies under regular review', but this implies current operations are not yet optimized.
findings.figures: 63p per £1 of rent income
findings.quote: Within 2026/27, net costs of management and repairs (after taking into account service charges and non-rent income) represents 63p of every £1 of rent income collected. We know that this is relatively high compared to benchmarks and will keep opportunities to seek greater efficiencies under regular review

findings.paper_title: HRA business plan and asset management strategy
findings.headline: £142 million additional borrowing for largest HRA investment programme in council's history
findings.detail: The council plans to invest £235m in housing stock over 30 years, with £142m financed through new borrowing on top of existing £67.5m debt from 2012. The council states this is sustainable based on 30-year assumptions, but represents a material increase in HRA debt levels.
findings.matters: This is a significant borrowing commitment that will increase the council's HRA debt substantially; lenders will want to understand whether the 30-year assumptions (especially rents and inflation) are robust.
findings.figures: £142m new borrowing; £235m total investment; £67.5m existing debt; £257.4m stock valuation
findings.quote: the HRA is projected to generate £854.5m income and invest £235m in the housing stock. This includes £142m financed through borrowing, which factors in the existing £67.5m debt originally taken out in 2012

findings.paper_title: SHDC Audit Annual Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account business plan has not been formally updated since 2013/14, and the council is now undertaking an external stock condition survey via Savills to inform long-term HRA financial planning.
findings.detail: The council's long-term HRA business plan was set in 2013/14 (over 11 years ago) and has since been amalgamated only into annual budget setting. In 2024/25, the council engaged Savills PLC to undertake a comprehensive Housing Stock Condition Survey for all council dwellings. The results will form an integral part of the long-term financial plan for the HRA. This indicates the council lacked current data on the condition and long-term maintenance requirements of its housing stock.
findings.matters: The HRA is a ring-fenced account with £14.8m of capital spending and £40.5m of council reserves partly supporting it. A 12-year-old business plan without recent stock condition data creates uncertainty about the true capital maintenance backlog and HRA sustainability. The need for an external review suggests prior planning was deficient.
findings.figures: HRA business plan last formally set 2013/14; HRA capital spend 2024/25 £14.8m; HRA budgeted surplus 2024/25 £669k, actual surplus £194k
findings.quote: The long-term Housing Revenue Account (HRA) business plan was set in 2013/14... The Council engaged Savills PLC, as an external expert, to undertake a review of the Housing Revenue Account stock throughout 2024/25. This information will be utilised for the Council to prepare a long-term financial plan for their HRA.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Audit Annual Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: The Section 151 officer departed in March 2025 during a period when the council's efficiency programme and financial control frameworks are being rebuilt.
findings.detail: The outgoing S151 officer left in March 2025 and had been heavily involved in discussion and updating of the efficiency savings long list. The audit notes that if processes, actions and priorities are not formally documented, there is a risk that key knowledge will be lost, hindering the council's ability to continue to effectively make savings. This departure coincides with internal audit finding insufficient controls in savings identification and monitoring.
findings.matters: The combination of S151 departure and unresolved efficiency programme governance means the council is entering 2025/26 (when it must deliver £1.2m of identified savings) with both new finance leadership and an ineffective savings tracking process.
findings.figures: Departure date March 2025; efficiency requirement 2025/26 £1.2m
findings.quote: The outgoing S151 officer was heavily involved in the discussion and updating of the long list and has left the organisation in March 2025. Therefore, if processes, actions and priorities are not formally documented, there is a risk to the Council that key knowledge will be lost.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Audit Annual Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: Capital programme delivery fell significantly short of budget in 2024/25, with general fund capital at 43% and HRA capital at 67% of planned spend.
findings.detail: As at end August 2024 (6 months into the year), the council had spent only £1.6m of an £11m general fund capital budget (15%) and £5.8m of a £22m HRA budget (26%). Despite forecasting a pick-up in the second half, final outturn was £4.8m general fund (43% of budget) and £14.8m HRA (67% of budget). This pattern suggests either project delays or constraints on capital deployment.
findings.matters: Systematic underperformance of capital programmes indicates either project delivery challenges or possible cash constraints. For a council already requiring efficiency savings, the ability to execute planned capital investment is a basic governance measure.
findings.figures: General fund budget £11m, actual £4.8m (43%); HRA budget £22m, actual £14.8m (67%). At Aug 2024: £1.6m of £11m (15%) and £5.8m of £22m (26%) spent
findings.quote: The Council is currently behind their capital programme for General Fund and Housing Revenue Account (HRA). They are reporting capital spend at the end of August 2024 of £1.6m and £5.8m against a full year budget of £11m and £22m respectively.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Audit Annual Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: The Internal Drainage Board levy creates an uncontrolled cost pressure growing at 30% average annually, with limited mitigation beyond annual £335k government support.
findings.detail: The IDB levy is budgeted at £3.4m for 2024/25, up 7.7% from the prior year. Historically the council has seen average increases of 30% between 2021/22 and the current period. The council estimates future increases at 5% per annum. The council received £335k of one-off government support for 2024/25 but is liaising with IDBs and lobbying government for longer-term relief, indicating the pressure is structural and beyond council control.
findings.matters: A cost that grows by 30% on average and represents 4% of the council's gross expenditure (£3.4m against £82m) cannot be offset by service efficiencies alone. This is a demand-driven cost with limited mitigation tools available to the council, creating structural budget risk.
findings.figures: £3.4m 2024/25 (7.7% increase from prior year); historical average increases of 30% from 2021/22; estimated future 5% annual increases; £335k government support 2024/25
findings.quote: The Internal Drainage Board (IDB) levy continues to be a cost pressure for the Council with a budgeted cost of £3.4m in 2024-25 (an increase of 7.7% from 2023/24). The Council has seen increases on average of 30% of the levy from 2021/22.

findings.paper_title: SHDC Audit Annual Report 2024 2025
findings.headline: The formal efficiency programme to deliver £1.8m in annual savings by 2028-29 is not operational and prior-year recommendations have not been implemented.
findings.detail: The council has no formal efficiency programme in place despite identifying this as a medium-risk issue in the prior year audit. The outgoing S151 officer, who left in March 2025, was heavily involved in updating the long list of potential efficiencies, and no formal documentation exists. The council achieved only 62% of its £832k efficiency target in 2024/25. September 2025 internal audit found insufficient controls in the savings identification and monitoring process.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver documented efficiency savings faces mounting pressure as the target grows from £0.8m (2024/25) to £1.8m (2028/29), with no clear mechanism to achieve them. Loss of the S151 officer knowledge and lack of formal tracking creates delivery risk on savings critical to budget balance.
findings.figures: £832k target 2024/25 (62% achieved); £1.2m required 2025/26; escalating to £1.8m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The efficiency programme we have obtained is a long list of potential efficiencies to be explored which are allocated to lead officers... There are no due dates on the efficiency list and therefore it cannot be seen if savings are falling behind plan. Therefore, based on audit evidence obtained for the year ended 31 March 2025, we have concluded that there is not a formal programme in place to effectively identify, RAG rate and monitor efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: Housing Landlord Service Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: Regulatory enforcement action and reputational damage risk if council fails to deliver improvement plan
findings.detail: The council is required to produce an improvement plan to address all C2 weaknesses. The risk section explicitly identifies that failure to deliver could trigger regulatory enforcement action, which would indicate governance failures and damage tenant trust in the council's largest landlord service.
findings.matters: Regulatory enforcement indicates deeper governance failures and potential credit implications; failure in a major service would affect council reputation and borrowing capacity
findings.figures: 3,800+ tenant households at risk
findings.quote: If the Council does not act on the improvement areas identified in the Regulator of Social Housing's (RSH) judgement, it risks non-compliance with statutory consumer standards. This could lead to reputational damage, regulatory enforcement action, and reduced tenant trust.

findings.paper_title: Housing Landlord Service Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: £735k already spent on housing improvements with £191k further planned for 2026/27 to address regulatory weaknesses
findings.detail: The council has invested £735k to date on housing service improvements required to address regulatory findings. An additional £191k is planned for 2026/27. These investments must be accommodated within the Housing Revenue Account's legal requirement to remain in balance.
findings.matters: Material HRA spending on regulatory compliance reduces financial flexibility and could constrain other council borrowing or investment capacity
findings.figures: £735k spent to date; £191k planned 2026/27
findings.quote: The total to date is £735k and further investments of £191k are in plan for financial year 2026/27 whilst ensuring that the HRA remains in balance as required by the relevant legislation.

findings.paper_title: Housing Landlord Service Regulatory Judgement
findings.headline: South Holland received a C2 regulatory grade on housing landlord services, indicating material weaknesses requiring improvement
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C2 grade following a programmed inspection from February to July 2025. A C2 grade means the regulator has identified material weaknesses likely to lead to poor tenant outcomes if not addressed. Weaknesses identified include incomplete stock condition surveys, tenant satisfaction with repairs, lack of formal tenant scrutiny mechanisms, and inconsistent approaches to vulnerable person data.
findings.matters: A regulatory downgrade on a major service (managing 3,800+ properties) indicates governance and service delivery weaknesses that affect council credit standing and could trigger regulatory enforcement
findings.figures: C2 grade; 3,800+ properties managed
findings.quote: C2- RSH judgement is that there are some weaknesses in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and improvement is needed.
